parts.title: Back and Forth, or One Way? Make the STRONGEST Nail Magnet (Part 2) | Stroke Method
parts.description:
Basil rubs his nail back and forth, with both ends of the magnet. Pip strokes his one way, with one pole. Which nail attracts more steel clips? Lock in your answer, be a steel paper clip, learn the three steps of the stroke method, spot the mistake on Pip's poster, and test whether more strokes make a stronger magnet, until the fishing game catches the big fish. Part 2 of Primary 3 Science, Making and Using Magnets: the stroke method.

In this part:
• Back and forth, or one way?
• Be a steel paper clip
• Look closer: lift up and away, the same direction
• Showdown: Pip's poster
• Look closer: ten, twenty or thirty strokes
• A chant to remember it all
• Spot the hidden ant!

Key words: same direction, same pole, stronger magnet.
Watch Part 1 first! Next episode: the magnet you can switch off.

TheOneApp, Explained: Singapore primary science, made fun. Play along with Pip, Basil and Momo: show fingers to lock in, keep score on your hand, beat the Buddies!

Can an iron nail become a magnet? P3 Science, Chapter 7, Making and Using Magnets (pp. 113 to 114): when a magnetic object becomes a magnet, we say that it has been magnetised; we can turn a magnetic object into a magnet by stroking it with a strong magnet: stroke the iron nail with one pole of a bar magnet, repeat the strokes in the same direction each time, and make sure to stroke the iron nail with the same pole; test it near some steel clips. The iron nail will become a stronger magnet when it is stroked more times with the magnet. The fourth episode of the Magnets theme. Also fits US NGSS 3-PS2-3 (Grade 3).
Safety and care: Nails are sharp: hold them by the head, and do this with an adult. Never put a magnet or a nail in your mouth, and keep magnets away from little brothers and sisters, phones and compasses. We look at woodpeckers and ants, and we do not touch them.
Try it at home: With an adult, stroke an iron nail with one end of a bar magnet from a science kit, from the head to the tip, lifting the magnet away each time. Do it thirty times, always the same way, with the same end. Put the magnet away, then see if the nail picks up a staple or a steel paper clip. Then try a nail stroked only ten times. (Use a bar magnet: a flat fridge magnet is too weak, and it has many poles.)
Iron nails from the neighbourhood hardware shop, and steel paper clips from the class stationery tray.
Grade 3 pupils in the US do the same experiment (NGSS 3-PS2-3), with a nail and a bar magnet from a science kit: stroke one way, with one pole, then test with paper clips.
